1.pericope_label: Make a joyful noise; serve the Lord with gladness

schools.summary: Augustine will not have the summons confined: the psalm exhorts no single corner of the earth, no one habitation or congregation, but exacts jubilance on every side because it has sown blessing on every side — does all the earth hear my voice at this moment, he asks, and yet the whole earth has heard this voice, so that what is not yet jubilant in the Lord will be.

Calvin takes the title for a summary of the contents, and sees in the indiscriminate invitation of the whole earth a prophecy of the time when the Church would be gathered out of many nations; Gill fills the shout with occasions — the angels at Christ's birth, the disciples at his entry into Jerusalem, the apostles at his ascension — and sets glad service against a slavish fear under a spirit of bondage.

Henry allows that the summons will be fully answered when all nations are discipled, but suspects the psalm was meant in the first place for proselytes who came over to the Jews' religion out of all lands; Spurgeon says the original word means a glad shout such as loyal subjects give when their king appears, holds that a happy God should be worshipped by a happy people, and calls the invitation no funeral solemnity but a bidding to a marriage feast.

Clarke corrects the received title — not a psalm of praise but one for the confession-offering, as the Chaldee, Vulgate, Septuagint and Ethiopic take it — reports the Syriac heading about Joshua the son of Nun, thinks the psalm composed after the captivity, and makes glad worship a duty as well as a privilege, since the man whom the religion of Christ has not made happy does not understand it.

Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm at the close of a series beginning with the ninety-first, marked by the mild sublimity and sunny cheerfulness they wonder at in the second part of Isaiah, and observe that this last Jubilate is entirely the echo of the first, proving the arrangement ingenious; they read the pilgrimage of all peoples to the holy mountain as an Old Testament dress for the hope of their conversion. Ellicott notes only that the phrase may be rendered all the earth.

sides.position: the whole earth without restriction, in prophecy of the Church gathered from many nations
in the first place proselytes who came over to the Jews’ religion out of all lands

themes: make a joyful noise, all ye lands
come before his presence with singing

3.pericope_label: Know that the Lord is God; enter into his gates

schools.summary: Gill reads the acknowledgment as a confession of Christ — own him God as well as man, and though a man yet no mere man but the great God and our Saviour, so a man as to be Jehovah's fellow — makes the gates those of Zion and so of the church and its public ordinances, and takes the goodness both providentially and in grace, Christ being the good Shepherd who laid down his life and the good Samaritan who pours wine and oil on wounds made by sin.

Clarke refuses the received text of the third verse, asking whether any people however heathenish could believe they had made themselves, and prefers the reading of twenty-six manuscripts, the Targum and the Masoretic margin, his we are; he keeps the emphasis on the privilege of public worship, notes again that the word rendered thanksgiving is properly the confession-offering, argues the closing attributes from the nature of God — mercy and compassion being modifications of a goodness essential to him, and therefore everlasting — and prints the psalm in Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Scottish with an interlineary translation.
Ellicott reports that most commentators now prefer 'his we are' as keeping the parallelism better and having great manuscript support, and notes that the close of the verse echoes an earlier psalm.

debates.question: Should the third verse read "and not we ourselves" or "and his we are"?

sides.position: 'his we are' — twenty-six manuscripts, the Targum, the Complutensian Polyglot and the Masoretic margin support it, and no people ever believed they made themselves
the negative stands in the present Hebrew text and in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Syriac
holders: the received text, reported by Clarke

themes: it is he that hath made us
and not we ourselves, or his we are
